title: The Snowball
intro: Last meeting you learned what interest is. Today you find out what it does when you leave it alone.

blocks.html:
Last meeting you learned the rule.

Interest is rent on money.

Save money, and the bank pays you rent for using it.

Borrow money, and you pay the rent instead.

And the rent is a percentage of the amount, every year.

Now here is the question nobody asked you last time.

You put £100 into the bank at 10% a year.

You earn your rent in the first year.

Then you leave it completely alone.

What happens in the second year?

Most adults get this wrong. Let us do it properly, one year at a time.

blocks.prompt:
Start with the easy year.

You put £100 in the bank. The bank pays 10% a year.
blocks.hint: 10% means divide by 10. Your very first gear, from Unit 1.

parts.label: Interest earned during year 1 (£)
parts._working: 10% of £100 = 100 ÷ 10 = £10. Her original 10% gear from w1s1, doing banking work.

parts.label: Total in the account at the end of year 1 (£)
parts._working: The £100 she put in, plus the £10 of interest: 100 + 10 = £110. Both parts are deliberately gentle — this is the early win, and the surprise is in the next question.

blocks.prompt:
Now year 2. You have not added a single penny of your own.

The bank pays 10% again.

But read that carefully. 10% of what?
blocks.hint: The bank pays 10% of whatever is sitting in the account at the start of the year. So what is sitting in there now — the £100 you put in, or something bigger?

parts.label: Interest earned during year 2 (£)
parts._working: At the start of year 2 the account holds £110, not £100. So the interest is 10% of £110 = 110 ÷ 10 = £11. This is the whole session in one number: £11, not £10.

parts.label: Total in the account at the end of year 2 (£)
parts._working: 110 + 11 = £121. Note she has earned £21 of interest in two years, not £20 — the extra £1 is interest paid ON her first year's interest.

blocks.html:
You spotted it.

Year 1 paid £10. Year 2 paid £11.

You did not add any money. So where did the extra pound come from?

The bank paid you interest on your interest.

Your £10 of interest from year 1 stayed in the account. So in year 2 it earned rent too.

Watch it happen across three years.

 Year 1Year 2Year 3
In the account at the start£100£110£121
Interest paid that year£10£11£12.10
In the account at the end£110£121£133.10

Every year the pile is bigger. So every year the rent is bigger.

The pile grows faster and faster, all by itself.

This has a name. It is called compound interest.

Compound just means the interest joins the pile and starts earning too.

People call it a snowball. A snowball rolling downhill picks up more snow, which makes it bigger, which means it picks up more snow still.

blocks.prompt:
Use the snowball on a bigger pot.

You save £200 at 10% a year, and you leave it alone for two years.
blocks.hint: Do year 1 first and write down the total. Then take 10% of that new total for year 2 — not 10% of the £200.

parts.label: Total in the account at the end of year 1 (£)
Total in the account at the end of year 2 (£)
parts._working: At the start of year 2 the pot holds £220. 10% of £220 = £22. 220 + 22 = £242. The year-2 interest is £22, not £20 — the snowball again. Common wrong answer would be £240 (adding £20 twice), which is exactly the mistake the session exists to prevent.

blocks.button: The same snowball, rolling the other way ✨
blocks.html:
Now the part the bank does not put on the poster.

A debt snowballs in exactly the same way.

Borrow £100 at 10%, and after one year you owe £110.

In year 2 the 10% is charged on the £110 you now owe.

So the debt grows faster and faster too — all by itself, while you do nothing.

The arithmetic is identical. Only the sign is flipped.

Saving: the snowball rolls towards you.

Borrowing: the snowball rolls at you.

You already know why this matters. It is how a small debt someone ignores becomes a big debt they cannot pay — and how trouble spreads from one borrower to the next.

blocks.prompt:
You borrow £100 on a card that charges 10% a year. You pay nothing back for two years.

In year 1 the card charges 10% of the £100 you borrowed. In year 2 it charges 10% of whatever you owe by then.
 Year 1Year 2
Owed at the start of the year£100?
Interest added that year??
blocks.hint: Exactly the same sums as your savings pot. The only difference is that this number is bad news instead of good news.

parts.label: Owed at the end of year 1 (£)
Owed at the end of year 2 (£)
parts._working: 10% of £110 = £11 added. 110 + 11 = £121 owed. Identical to her savings answer in s2 — deliberately, so the mirror is impossible to miss. She has paid nothing and now owes £21 more than she borrowed.

blocks.prompt:
Boss question. Two sisters each handle £500 for two years, at 10% a year.

One sister saves her £500 in the bank and never touches it.

The other sister borrows £500 and never pays any of it back.
 At the startEnd of year 1End of year 2
Sister who saves — pot£500£550?
Sister who borrows — debt£500£550?
blocks.hint: The first year is done for you — 10% of £500 is £50. Now do the second year on the new amount, £550. Then notice that you only have to do that sum once.

parts.label: The saving sister's pot at the end of year 2 (£)
The borrowing sister's debt at the end of year 2 (£)
parts._working: Identical arithmetic: £605. That is the point of the question — one sister HAS £605 and the other OWES £605, from the same sum. Same maths, opposite life.

parts.label: How much interest did the saving sister earn over the two years altogether? (£)
parts._working: 605 − 500 = £105. Cross-check by adding the two years: £50 in year 1 plus £55 in year 2 = £105 ✓. Worth noticing it is not £100 — the extra £5 is the interest her first year's interest earned.

blocks.prompt:
★ The analyst's puzzle. You have £100 and two offers.

The first offer pays 20%, but only for one year. Then it stops.

The second offer pays 10%, and it runs for two years, snowballing.

Twice the rate for half the time. Which ends up bigger?
 At the startEnd of year 1End of year 2
20% for one year£100?it has stopped
10% for two years£100£110?
blocks.hint: Work out each one on its own. For the 20% offer, 20% is double your 10% gear. For the 10% offer you already know the answer from the start of this session.

parts.label: The 20% offer: total at the end of year 1 (£)
parts._working: 20% of £100 = £20 (double the 10% gear). 100 + 20 = £120, and then it stops.

parts.label: The 10% offer: total at the end of year 2 (£)
parts._working: £110 after year 1, then 10% of £110 = £11, giving £121. Same figure she worked out in s2 — the callback is intentional.

parts.label: How much bigger is the winner? (£)
parts._working: 121 − 120 = £1. The snowball wins — but only just. One single pound. That thinness is the lesson: compounding does not win by a landslide over two years, it wins by a whisker. Its power is TIME, not drama. Over twenty years that whisker becomes an avalanche, which is what the summit asks her to think about.

blocks.html:
📈 Dinner-table magic trick:

Bankers have a shortcut for the snowball. It is called the rule of 72.

Divide 72 by the interest rate. The answer is roughly how many years your money takes to double.

At 10%, that is 72 ÷ 10, which is about 7 years.

Your job tonight: test it. Start with £100 and roll the snowball forward, year by year, on paper. Round to the nearest pound each year — it keeps every sum inside your 10% gear, and it is plenty accurate enough.

Does it really reach £200 at around year 7? (Watch carefully. It gets close to £200 at year 7 and passes it at year 8. So is the rule wrong, or near enough?)

Then try the trick at 20%, and at 5%. Ask Dad which he would rather have: 5% for thirty years, or 20% for five years. Work out both before either of you answers.

And the real question, the one your ★ was pointing at: if compounding only won by £1 over two years, how can anyone call it powerful?

done.title: Meeting adjourned ✓
done.html:
Compound interest. The snowball.

You know why year 2 pays more than year 1, and you can roll a pot forward year by year without being fooled into adding the same interest twice.

You also know the hard half: a debt snowballs with exactly the same arithmetic, rolling the other way, while the borrower does nothing at all.

Next: Market Story: The 0% Offer — a credit card that charges you nothing for a whole year. You are going to read the small print and tell the board what it really costs.
